#9837. Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Discovered using AI, the memory corruption vulnerability affects the OpenJDK runtime and could allow unauthenticated attackers to take over systems.

A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.

The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.

However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.

Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.

The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages.

"To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."

Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters.

"For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."

Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Much like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.

Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.

Fortunately for defenders, Java4Shell should not quite have the impact that Log4Shell did and still does, though it doesn't mean they shouldn't take Java4Shell very seriously, Duong tells Dark Reading.

"Log4Shell was very easy to exploit," he says. "Java4Shell [is] harder. However, we're comparing a 10 to a 9. They are both very bad; Log4Shell was just worse."

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Both flaws also highlight the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps.

"Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions provider Black Duck.

The practical problem now for organizations "is that exposure depends on the Java build, the processor and how an application handles input, and many teams cannot answer those questions quickly, especially for JDKs bundled inside applications and containers," he says.

Because flaws like these are so deeply embedded, they may go undiscovered and remain critical security gaps. In this case, the use of AI to uncover Java4Shell potentially may have helped the industry avert disaster, giving organizations time to patch before it's been widely exploited, notes James Matchett, head of security at Cloudsmith.

"Its discovery shows how AI can uncover weaknesses in widely used software that might otherwise have gone undetected for years," he says.

Indeed, Java4Shell's discovery iillustrates how AI can speed up vulnerability discovery.

"An AI coding assistant found this bug in about an hour and a first working exploit took two more, for under $200 in tokens," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering for cybersecurity firm Secure.com, tells Dark Reading. "The flaw sat in one of the most-audited runtimes there is. That is what discovery looks like now: cheap, fast, and available to defenders and attackers alike."

However, Matchett says the flip side is it also can help attackers move more quickly to weaponize security flaws, noting that organizations are under intense pressure to find and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. As Ahmed puts it, "defenders now have less time between a bug being found and being used."

There is little doubt that defenders should take the Java4Shell seriously. Calif researchers demonstrated RCE in a laundry list of widely deployed Java applications in their default configurations, noting that they, too, used AI to develop exploits, Luong wrote.

The team achieved pre-authorization RCE in the following: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Meanwhile, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are vulnerable to post-auth RCE, they said.

"The lists are non-exhaustive," Luong wrote. "We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested."

An independent researcher also shared with Calif a client-side exploit that demonstrates how "a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own," Luong wrote.

As mentioned, organizations should start mitigations as soon as possible, with patching Internet-facing applications as the top priority, and internal apps second, Luong tells Dark Reading. Calif will wait at least one-to-two weeks before releasing any app-specific exploit code to allow for defenders to upgrade.

"Thanksgiving is also coming, [and] everyone needs a break," he says.

Organizations also can mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with one of the following flags: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512, Luong advised.

The second should only be applied on x86-64 hosts, as OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and thus won't start the system, he added.

Black Duck's Glavach recommends that organizations start their mitigation process with conducting an inventory, patching Internet-facing identity and build systems first, and staying clear of unverified fixes and fake exploits circulating online.

Secure.com's Ahmed was even more specific, advising that organizations "find every server running Java 17.0.6 or later, patch the ones open to the Internet first, and turn off the Base64 intrinsic where you can't patch yet."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9835. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9833. AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

Analysis of 20 Iranian state-sponsored threat groups details how espionage, ransomware, and hacktivism intersect in state-backed cyber campaigns.

ANTA CLARA, Calif. — (BUSINESS WIRE) — AttackIQ, the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), today released new research that connects previously fragmented reporting on individual Iranian cyber campaigns to map the relationships among state-sponsored operators and the institutions supporting them. The findings show Iranian espionage groups turn compromised networks into launchpads for other operators, transforming intelligence-gathering operations into destructive attacks.

Threat reporting on Iran typically covers one campaign at a time, and vendors track the same groups under different names. Helix Kitten alone appears under eight other names, including OilRig, APT34 and Scarred Manticore. AttackIQ’s Adversary Research Team consolidated that reporting into Weighing Cyber Power: Evaluating the Strategic and Operational Significance of Iran’s State-Sponsored Cyber Capability, a single map of 20 Iranian adversaries, the government institutions they are linked to and the contractors that supply their personnel, tooling and infrastructure.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

“The value of threat research is measured by the decisions it informs,” said Paul Reid, VP of Adversary Research at AttackIQ. “Understanding which Iranian groups work together, and how confident we can be in each relationship, gives defenders a clear starting point for emulation and a realistic picture of what could follow an initial compromise. It turns a single detection into a forecast of what comes next.”

The report traces how a single intrusion can pass between groups. In one documented case, Helix Kitten (Scarred Manticore), conducted prolonged intelligence collection inside a network before handing off the network access to Banished Kitten (Void Manticore), which pursued destructive objectives. In a second case, Static Kitten (Mango Sandstorm) established access and passed it to Storm-1084, a destructive operator. In a separate campaign against the Albanian government, four separately tracked groups contributed to the same operation, which spanned reconnaissance, initial access, data theft and the deployment of destructive tooling.

When the damage arrives, it is frequently disguised. The research also found Iranian groups staging destructive attacks as ransomware or hacktivism, obscuring the intent behind the attacks. Pioneer Kitten provided criminal ransomware affiliates with access to compromised networks.

The organizations hit first may be a route to other targets. Several groups can gain access to more heavily defended organizations, including in the defense industrial base, through their subsidiaries, contractors, and suppliers.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

The analysis classifies 20 Iranian adversaries into three weight classes based on their organizational significance, operational relevance, and demonstrated capabilities. The classifications underscore that even smaller, specialized groups can play critical roles in larger cyber campaigns.

Heavyweight: Established groups with sustained espionage operations, internally developed tooling and a central role in Iran’s cyber strategy.

Lightweight: Groups with more focused missions, including specialized espionage, access facilitation and destructive operations.

Featherweight: Groups with narrower or less consistently documented activity, some relying on support from more established adversaries.

“Iran isn’t as technically sophisticated as China, Russia or North Korea, but what it lacks in sophistication it makes up for in cadence,” said Francis Guibernau, Senior Adversary Research Engineer at AttackIQ. “They target anything and everything, on every operating system and in industrial environments. That volume, combined with how freely these groups share access, is what makes the ecosystem dangerous.”

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

The research draws on more than 200 references and consolidates more than 2,600 procedures, 1,300 file indicators, and 2,300 network indicators. The analysis was also validated against threat intelligence and real-world activity observed by several Fortune 150 companies actively targeted by Iranian threat actors. The research team also received input from National Computer Incident Response Teams (CIRTs) and members of the intelligence community.

To help organizations put the research into practice, AttackIQ will be releasing adversary emulations based on the documented tactics, techniques, and procedures of Iranian threat actors over the coming weeks. These emulations will enable security teams to safely test their defenses against relevant adversary behaviors, identify gaps in detection and prevention, and prioritize improvements based on real-world threat intelligence.

For a closer look at the findings with AttackIQ’s adversary research team, join the December 10 webinar, Breaking Down Iran’s Most Dangerous Cyber Tactics.

AttackIQ is the leader in threat-informed Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM), helping organizations continuously validate defenses, break attack paths, and reduce threat debt through evidence-based security operations.

Through AVA Agentic OS, AttackIQ has introduced the industry’s first agentic operating system purpose-built for CTEM, enabling organizations to execute Continuous Threat Exposure Management autonomously at enterprise scale.

By orchestrating specialized AI agents across threat intelligence, adversary exposure validation, security validation, detection engineering, control optimization, threat debt reduction, and AI security validation, AttackIQ transforms fragmented security activities into continuous cyber resilience.

Trusted by the world’s largest enterprises, government agencies, and managed security providers, AttackIQ empowers organizations to continuously discover, validate, and reduce cyber risk with confidence.

#9831. Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

New agentic AI solution leverages APIs to collect compliance evidence from systems and applies it to over 30 frameworks with no duplicate work.

SEATTLE, November 18, 2026 — Strike Graph, the enterprise AI-native governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) management platform, today announced a new integration solution that seamlessly connects to any software API to automatically collect compliance evidence from it. With Integration AI, organizations using the Strike Graph platform are no longer limited to a fixed integration catalog. They simply indicate the system they are using and Strike Graph builds a native integration that pulls compliance evidence from it automatically.

Once connected via an API, the Strike Graph platform employs an AI research agent to read the vendor’s public API documentation and draft a build specification. Concurrently, a second AI agent builds the complete integration across Strike Graph’s backend, user interface, and evidence pipeline. Integrations connect API-to-API, and customers never install agents or software inside their own infrastructure, which is critical for maintaining enterprise-grade security.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

“For compliance to be successful, access to evidence must be quick, easy, and continuous, but integration with existing tools often presents a challenge,” said Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. “Integration AI has empowered Strike Graph to overcome those roadblocks and accomplish all three of those requirements at once. If it has an API, Strike Graph can collect evidence from it. Furthermore, since Strike Graph’s evidence model is graph-based, evidence from a newly built integration automatically counts toward every framework a customer pursues, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, with no duplicate work.”

As with all Strike Graph evidence collection integrations, Integration AI builds secure integrations that are restricted to read-only operations by default. Each one carries an endpoint allowlist that ratifies against the vendor’s real API documentation, which guarantees evidence collection can observe a customer’s systems but never change or impact them.

Strike Graph keeps strict separation where credentials are never touched by Integration AI.The build process works outside of the core governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) program itself, building the connection with no access to any customer secrets. Credentials and other sensitive data live in a securely managed secrets vault, and the build spec is scanned and automatically rejected if any credentials are detected in it.

With Integration AI, vendor documentation is treated strictly as data and never as instructions, which blocks prompt-injection attempts hidden in third-party content. The AI build environment holds no publishing rights, and a separate locked-down step does the publishing.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

Builds sit behind an approver allowlist and a kill switch, and humans are always in the loop to review the research plan before build starts, after code has been written, and before anything is deployed to production. The AI can only propose changes, not ship them, and every integration requires a human engineering review.

Once built, Integration AI runs evidence scripts in self-contained isolated sandbox environments with no shared code paths, so a flaw in one integration can’t spread to another.

Integration AI is available to Strike Graph customers today. For more information, visit www.strikegraph.com.

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Where Americans fall on the income spectrum — Pew Research Center 2026 data.

National median household income — the midpoint dividing upper and lower halves

Share of U.S. households classified as upper income by Pew Research

How much location can shift income class thresholds between cheapest and costliest metros

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Use these calculators to see where you stand on your FI journey.

Find out how much you need to reach financial independence.

See if your current investments can coast to your retirement target.

Your savings rate matters more than returns. See where you are.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

#9828. Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

The state-sponsored threat group is using data stolen from one victim to target others via convincing impersonations and social engineering attacks.

The Russian cyber-espionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships.

It's a tactic that researchers at Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) observed the attacker deploy with clinical efficiency in two separate compromises involving US organizations over the past year.

In the first intrusion, late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic actors later used that material to impersonate an employee of the first organization for a successful social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization.

The activity, GTIG researchers said, shows how traditional social engineering is becoming more closely tied to attacks on cloud identities. Once inside an organization's cloud environment, an attacker can gather the kind of internal information that makes a message from a supposedly trusted colleague or business contact much harder to spot as a scam.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," GTIG researchers wrote in a blog post. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."

Cold Relic (also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto, and Gossamer Bear) is a cyber-espionage group that Google researchers have been tracking — and disrupting — since 2015. The US government has assessed the outfit as working within Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) and tasked with collecting information of political and strategic interest to Moscow.

Though low-profile, Cold Relic has notched up numerous high-value targets including defense contractors, government officials, and NGOs across North America and Europe. One of its favorite post-compromise activities, according to GTIG, is to steal emails and data that can help it establish "authentic pretexts" and convincing impersonations when reaching out to other potential targets.

In the first intrusion in late 2025, Cold Relic used stolen credentials for a super admin account to access a US organization's cloud environment. The attackers routed their activity through a residential proxy located near the organization, so their connections appeared to originate from a familiar geographic area. The attacker repeatedly kept sending the actual account holder multifactor authentication (MFA) push notifications until the overwhelmed user approved one.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

After gaining access, Cold Relic actors registered their own device on the network and established additional ways to authenticate to it, including via passkeys, backup MFA codes, and additional rogue MFA devices. The threat group used the stolen Super Admin user privileges to exfiltrate the organization's cloud storage, including full employee lists, email conversations, and organizational directories and contact lists. The threat actors then initiated several anti-forensics measures that allowed it to maintain access to the compromised network for several months.

In the second attack, earlier this year, Cold Relic impersonated an employee of the first company to contact an individual at a second organization through an encrypted messaging app. The threat actors sent the unsuspecting target phishing links disguised as documents relevant to their ongoing conversation.

After stealing the victim's Microsoft Entra ID credentials and authentication tokens, Cold Relic used them to access the organization's Google Workspace environment through its federated single sign-on system. The attackers then helped themselves to files from the compromised user's cloud drive while also seeking out email archives, chat records, credentials, personnel information, and other data of potential intelligence value.

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

"Cold Relic is highly adept at leveraging social networks and impersonation of key individuals to achieve a realistic pretense for reaching out to the targeted individual or organization," Wes Shields, security engineer at GTIG, tells Dark Reading. "Once they have achieved their initial access goal, they move quickly to maintain persistence and exfiltrate data."

The lesson for organizations is to train employees to be wary of unexpected messages, particularly when they arrive through communication channels a supposed colleague or business contact doesn't normally use. If a message seems unusual, employees should verify the sender's identity through a separate, previously established channel before responding or acting on it, Shields advises.

"In today's hyper-connected world, it is impossible to have employees not be reachable via multiple channels, and attackers are taking advantage of this," he says.

Joseph Spero, principal incident response consultant at Google, recommends other measures to limit the damage from identity-based attacks. These include enforcing phishing-resistant MFA, restricting and auditing passkey registrations, hardening MFA registration procedures, and auditing OAuth grants.

"Short-lived sessions and the principle of least privilege will limit the potential scope of access when credentials are compromised," he says. "When a compromise is suspected, mandate session revocation in addition to resetting passwords and MFA mechanisms."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9826. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9824. Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Nigeria faced more than double the cyber threats of the previous year, with Angola and Kenya also in the top 5 most-attacked countries globally.

Organizations in Africa faced an average of 3,834 cyberattacks per week in October, a jump of 38% from a year earlier, making the continent the most-attacked region for the first time in more than a year.

Nigeria, Angola, and Kenya were among the top-five most targeted countries, with Nigeria topping the list with nearly 6,700 attacks targeting organizations in the country every week; that marks a 140% increase over October 2025, according to data published by Check Point Research earlier this month. The nations are among those rapidly pushing technological transformation of their infrastructure, expanding connectivity, investing in digital services, and putting sensitive data in network-connected applications and storage.

The fast transformation is exposing more opportunities for attackers, says Shayimamba Conco, chief technology officer and security evangelist in the Office of the CTO at Check Point Software.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

"All this rapid digital expansion is now happening within the region, but then, at the same time, this [expansion] is outpacing improvements in security maturity," he says, adding that security improvements are uneven across the continent. "Yes, some areas — let's say for example, South Africa — it's adopting cybersecurity at a much quicker rate than the rest of the Africa region, but there will be those regions which are still lagging behind a bit."

The significant increase in average weekly attacks pushed African organizations past those in Latin America as the favored targets of cyberattackers. In the first quarter of 2026, Latin America averaged more than 3,000 attacks per week, surpassing the approximate 2,700 attacks targeting African organizations. In September, the two regions essentially tied in terms of attacks, with Africa once again becoming the most popular target in October.

Globally, organizations experienced an average of 2,550 weekly cyberattacks in October, down 9% from September but up a third from the previous year. While Africa encountered the most weekly attacks, both Latin America and Asia-Pacific regions saw a greater-than-average number — 3,483 and 3,436, respectively.

Globally, cyberattacks focused heavily on the education sector, with the average academic institution suffering more than 5,900 attacks per week, up a third from the same month in 2025. The education sector has topped the global list of popular targets every month, with organizations made attractive to attackers because of their large data sets and reliance on legacy systems, says Conco.

Related:Malicious Linux Implants Mimic Asian Mail Security Products

"There is a lack of budget when it comes to not just IT, but specifically cybersecurity," he says. "A junior IT engineer has to manage these vast environments, which are hard to lock down by nature, because you've got all these students who need access to all these applications and resources."

In Africa, however, cyberattackers most often targeted financial services, government agencies, and the energy sector, according to Check Point's data.

The countries are racing to improve their cybersecurity postures and address persistent threats. Nigeria's National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) continues to work on the details of the nation's cybersecurity and cloud-sovereignty policies. Last month, Operation Serengeti 3.0 — a joint task force between Interpol and 20 African countries — led to the arrest of more than 1,500 suspects and the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds. In August, Operation Jackal IV targeted West African crime syndicates, leading to more than 200 arrests.

Check Point also flagged the use of AI in companies as a potential weak point, finding that about 2.9% of prompts to generative AI and large language models (LLMs) posed a high risk of leaking sensitive information. The risk is steadily increasing over time, from 2.3% in August to 2.5% in September.

Related:UAE, Saudi Arabia Face Onslaught of Increasingly Complex Cyberattacks

Interpol has also observed that attackers are increasingly using AI in a way that has impacted African nations. In its African Cybercrime Assessment Report 2026, Interpol found that 55% of reported cybercrimes across Africa used AI to some degree.

"Cybercrime has emerged as one of the most significant criminal threats to the region," Neal Jetton, Director of Interpol’s Cybercrime unit, said in a statement in August. "AI is automating every stage of a cyberattack from reconnaissance and phishing to extortion and evasion. However, we see that when countries work together, cybercriminal infrastructure can be identified, disrupted and dismantled."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9823. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9822. Why Holiday Security Can't Wait for Black Friday

Bot-driven fraud and holiday social engineering attacks stretch across many weeks, straining security teams and small businesses alike.

Cyber experts have long drawn connections between the accelerated volumes of holiday shopping and threat actors looking for opportunities to take advantage, but as the festive season kicks off, it's important to remember that security posture during this time period is a marathon — not a sprint.

Verizon today published survey results for its holiday trends report, tracking the insights of 600 small business owners and decision-makers in the US. Of those surveyed, 11% said they have dealt with a cyberattack or data-security incident during the holidays, and a third expect to increase cybersecurity investments this holiday season compared with last year.

Meanwhile, managed security services firm VikingCloud this week published a report surveying security and IT leaders which made even steeper claims: a full 86% of respondents said their business has faced at least one successful cyberattack in the past 12 months, and a whopping 98% said at least one came during the 2025 holiday season. And the Retail & Hospitality Information Sharing and Analysis Center (RH-ISAC) last year said the holiday season continues to be the most active fraud environment from a defender standpoint.

Related:In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools, Maybe More

Some reasons behind the prominence of cyberattacks during this time period are straightforward: Many cybersecurity teams experience lighter staffing during holiday periods and weekends (leaving the door open for easier ransomware attacks). The chaos of the holiday season also means online services and retailers are inundated with activity, giving threat actors cover. And on the social engineering front, the holidays give plenty of pretext for threat actors conducting phishing campaigns (fake emails promising unbelievable Black Friday deals, charity scams, and so on).

Some teams may take this as a cue to prepare for a few select days or weeks of this last part of the year, such as Black Friday or the week leading up to Christmas. But new research around one narrow corner of the threat landscape suggests that may not be wise.

One of the less-discussed types of threat activity retailers face each season is an influx of malicious bots.

F5 today published a study dedicated to automated threat activity leading up to Black Friday. The report analyzed bot and automation traffic across three Black Friday shopping seasons (2023 to 2025) using data from F5 Distributed Cloud Bot Defense. It covers retailers in three retail sub-industries: fashion, e-commerce, and quick-service restaurants (QSR). The report's authors observed that overall automation rose across the three seasons, from 17.4% of transactions in 2023 to 18.5% in 2024, and then 28.6% in 2025.

Related:As Test Takers Turn to AI, Exam Security Plays Catch-Up

The types of activity differ across industries, but F5 observed bots being used for product scraping and inventory hoarding, credential stuffing and account takeover, fake account creation (to claim new user offers), and gift card cracking (inserting gift card numbers into balance checkers to test for valid accounts).

In terms of trends overall, cyberattackers are increasingly leaning toward Web stores over mobile APIs, and a broad rise in bot sophistication over time. But one of the most notable conclusions that F5 researchers made is that there's no single best date to defend. Attackers start their bot onslaught weeks before Black Friday, and continue it well into the weeks after.

As Sean Murphy, F5's field chief information security officer (CISO) for North America, tells Dark Reading, "The data shows that automated activity can be elevated well before the shopping weekend, and the busiest day for automation varied dramatically from year to year."

Bot traffic does not necessarily reflect all threat activity, but there may be a broader lesson here: that steeling your security hygiene for the holiday season is not a few single days or weekends to prepare for but a broader stretch of time that spans from early November to the end of the year. Murphy says security teams "should have monitoring and protections in place throughout the shopping season rather than scaling them up only for Thanksgiving week."

Related:Attackers in Binance Breach Targeted Known Weakness, Missing Controls

For those in ecommerce dealing with Web and mobile APIs, he urges ensuring protection isn't substantially weaker on one than the other.

"Web traffic had much higher automation rates among the retailers studied, but the report specifically cautions against interpreting that as evidence that APIs are inherently safer. Where API protection is weaker, attackers can shift toward that channel," he says. "And because the dataset contains both simple scripts and automation designed to imitate legitimate users, defenses need to account for a spectrum of bot sophistication rather than relying on a single detection technique."

Finally, he recommends organizations prioritize targeted employee security awareness and training, particularly for those teams handling customer accounts, payments, and other sensitive information. "Many attacks still begin with social engineering and credential theft, so employees need to know how to recognize suspicious requests and protect account access."

Chris Flood, senior vice president and CRO of Verizon Business, tells Dark Reading that small businesses can reduce their risk with four fairly simple steps: require multifactor authentication, train employees how to spot scams, keep guest Wi-Fi separate from payment systems, and keep software and devices updated.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.
